      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Female Infertility</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Infertility, Female</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Infertility means not being able to get pregnant after at least one year of trying (or 6 months if the woman is over age 35). If a woman keeps having miscarriages, it is also called <span class="qt0">infertility.  Female infertility</span> can result from age, physical problems, hormone problems, and lifestyle or environmental factors.</p><p>Most cases of infertility in women result from problems with producing eggs. In primary ovarian insufficiency, the ovaries stop functioning before natural menopause.  In polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the ovaries may not release an egg regularly or they may not release a healthy egg.</p><p>About a third of the time, infertility is because of a problem with the woman. One third of the time, it is a problem with the man. Sometimes no cause can be found.</p><p>If you think you might be infertile, see your doctor. There are tests that may tell if you have fertility problems. When it is possible to find the cause, treatments may include medicines, surgery, or assisted reproductive technologies. Happily, many couples treated for infertility are able to have babies.</p><p>Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/infertility.html">
      <content name="title">Infertility</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Artificial Insemination</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Fertility</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Gamete Intrafallopian Transfer</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sterility</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is infertility?<p>Infertility means not becoming pregnant after having frequent, unprotected sex for one year or longer. If you are age 35 or older, infertility can be diagnosed after six months. Infertility also includes situations where you can get pregnant, but the pregnancy ends in repeated miscarriage or stillbirth.</p><p>Infertility is common. It can affect both men and women. Sometimes both partners contribute to the cause.</p>What causes infertility?<p>Infertility can happen because of a health issue in you or your partner or a mix of factors. In some cases, no clear cause is found.</p>Common causes in women include:<ul><li>Failure to ovulate, often due to conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)</li><li>Blocked or damaged fallopian tubes (the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus), often caused by past sexually transmitted infections (STIs), pelvic inflammatory disease, or abdominal (belly) surgery</li><li>Conditions affecting the uterus (womb), such as fibroids or endometriosis</li><li>Problems producing eggs, which may occur with aging</li><li>Hormonalimbalances, such as having too much estrogen</li></ul>Common causes in men include:<ul><li>Low sperm count</li><li>Sperm that doesn't move well</li><li>Blocked sperm ducts</li><li>Hormonal imbalances, such as having too much testosterone</li></ul><p>Certain lifestyle habits can also raise your risk of infertility. These can include smoking, heavy alcohol use, and being very overweight or underweight. Older age and some health conditions may increase your risk as well.</p>How is infertility diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider will ask about your health history and may do a physical exam. Testing is different for women and men. It may include blood tests, imaging tests, and a semen test for men.</p>How is infertility treated?<p>Treatment depends on the cause, how long you've been trying to get pregnant, and your age. Some treatments are for men, some are for women, and some involve both partners. Common options include treatment for the underlying cause, medicines,assisted reproductive technology, and surgery.</p><p>Infertility can be stressful. Counseling and support groups may help you and your partner cope. Many couples who receive treatment go on to have children.</p>Can infertility be prevented?<p>Not all cases of infertility can be prevented, but practicing healthy habits may help lower your risk:</p><ul><li>Quit smoking, or don't start</li><li>Limitalcohol</li><li>Maintain a healthy weight</li><li>Practice safe sex to prevent STIs, except when you're trying to get pregnant</li></ul><p>If you're ready to try to get pregnant, see your provider if you are over age 40, haveirregular periods, have a history of pelvic inflammatory disease, or have had fertility concerns in the past.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/endometriosis.html">
      <content name="title">Endometriosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Adenomyosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Endo</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is endometriosis?<p>The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. The uterus is lined with tissue (endometrium). Endometriosis is a disease in which tissue like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body. These patches of tissue are called "implants," "nodules," or "lesions." They are most often found:</p><ul><li>On or under the ovaries</li><li>On the fallopian tubes, which carry eggs from the ovaries to the uterus</li><li>Behind the uterus</li><li>On the tissues that hold the uterus in place</li><li>On the bowels or bladder</li></ul><p>In rare cases, the tissue may grow on your lungs or in other parts of your body.</p>What causes endometriosis?<p>Researchers don't know what causes endometriosis.</p>Who is at risk for endometriosis?<p>Endometriosis can affect anyone who menstruates. Certain factors can raise or lower your risk of getting it.</p><p>You are at higher risk if:</p><ul><li>You have a mother, sister, or daughter with endometriosis</li><li>Your period started before age 11</li><li>Your monthly cycles are short (less than 27 days)</li><li>Your menstrual cycles are heavy and last more than 7 days</li></ul><p>You have a lower risk if:</p><ul><li>You have been pregnant before</li><li>Your periods started late in adolescence</li><li>You breastfeed your babies</li></ul>What are the symptoms of endometriosis?<p>The main symptoms of endometriosis are:</p><ul><li>Pelvic pain, which often happens during your period</li><li>Infertility</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Painful menstrual cramps, which may get worse over time</li><li>Pain during or after sex</li><li>Pain in the intestine or lower abdomen</li><li>Pain with bowel movements (pooping) or urination (peeing), usually during your period</li><li>Heavy periods</li><li>Spotting or bleeding between periods</li><li>Digestive or gastrointestinal symptoms</li><li>Fatigue or lack of energy</li></ul>How is endometriosis diagnosed?<p>Surgery is the only way to know for sure that you have endometriosis. First, however, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. You will have a pelvic exam and may have some imaging tests.</p><p>The most common surgery to diagnose endometriosis is a laparoscopy. This is a type of surgery that uses a laparoscope, a thin tube with a camera and light. The surgeon inserts the laparoscope through a small cut in the skin near your belly button. Your provider can make a diagnosis based on how the patches of endometriosis look. They may also do a biopsy to get a tissue sample.</p>What are the treatments for endometriosis?<p>There is no cure for endometriosis, but there are treatments for the symptoms. Your provider will work with you to decide which treatments would be best for you.</p><p>Treatments for endometriosis pain include:</p><ul><li>Pain relievers, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) such as ibuprofen and a prescription medicine specifically for endometriosis. Providers may sometimes prescribe opioids for severe pain.</li><li>Hormone therapy, which stops the ovaries from making hormones. This may slow the growth of the endometrial tissue and may stop new areas from growing. Types of hormone therapy include: 
	<ul><li>Birth control pills.</li><li>Progestin therapy.</li><li>Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) medicines (GnRH agonists and antagonists).  These medicines cause a temporary menopause.  After your stop taking the medicines, your menstrual periods will start again, and pregnancy is possible.</li></ul></li><li>Surgical treatments for severe pain, including procedures to remove the endometriosis patches or cut some nerves in the pelvis. The surgery may be a laparoscopy or major surgery.</li></ul><p>Treatments for infertility caused by endometriosis include:</p><ul><li>Laparoscopy to remove the endometriosis patches</li><li>In vitro fertilization</li><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></ul></content>

      <content name="title">Male Infertility</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Infertility, Male</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Low Sperm Count</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Infertility is a term doctors use if a man hasn't been able to get a woman pregnant after at least one year of trying. Causes of male infertility include:</p><ul><li>Physical problems with the testicles</li><li>Blockages in the ducts that carry sperm</li><li>Hormone problems</li><li>A history of high fevers or mumps</li><li>Genetic disorders</li><li>Lifestyle or environmental factors</li></ul><p>About a third of the time, infertility is because of a problem with the man. One third of the time, it is a problem with the woman. Sometimes no cause can be found.</p><p>If you suspect you are infertile, see your doctor. There are tests that may tell if you have fertility problems. When it is possible to find the cause, treatments may include medicines, surgery, or assisted reproductive technology. Happily, many couples treated for infertility are able to have babies.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>
